lead: An NMOS inverter is one nMOS driver pulling the output down plus a load pulling it up. The driver alone cannot make a logic high, so the load sets output levels. Four loads are common: resistor, enhancement nMOS with gate at V<sub>DD</sub>, depletion nMOS with gate at its source, and pMOS with gate at ground (pseudo-nMOS). Each gives different V<sub>OL</sub>, V<sub>OH</sub> and static current. Old NMOS chips used these; today they appear as ratioed logic and weak pull-ups inside CMOS blocks.
prereq: You need the nMOS linear and saturation current equations from Unit 1, and the voltage transfer curve and noise-margin definitions from 3.1.

sections.h3: The load line and the resistive load

blocks.text: The driver is a single nMOS: drain at the output, source at ground, gate at the input. It can only pull down. The load pulls up.

With a resistor R<sub>L</sub> from V<sub>DD</sub> to the output, the load current is I = (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>out</sub>)/R<sub>L</sub>. On the driver's I-V curves this is a straight line through (V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>, I = 0) with slope −1/R<sub>L</sub>. Each input voltage selects one driver curve; where that curve crosses the load line is the operating point.
V<sub>in</sub> = 0: the driver is off, no current flows, so V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>.

V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>: the driver sinks current while holding the output low. The crossing lies in the linear region, because V<sub>OL</sub> is small compared with V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. Equate the two currents:

blocks.where: V<sub>DD</sub> is the supply in volts, R<sub>L</sub> the load resistor in ohms, k<sub>n</sub> = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>(W/L) the driver gain in A/V², V<sub>tn</sub> the driver threshold in volts, V<sub>OL</sub> the output low voltage. The left side is the resistor current, the right side the linear-region driver current.

blocks.text: A small V<sub>OL</sub> needs a large R<sub>L</sub> and a wide driver. A 100 kΩ resistor is far larger than a transistor and draws current whenever the output is low: tens of microamperes per gate at 5 V, so ten thousand gates burn watts. A transistor load replaced it, small and ratioed by width.
Enhancement load. An nMOS with drain at VDD, source at the output and gate at VDD. Then VGS = VDD − Vout, so it conducts strongly only while the output is well below VDD.

With V<sub>in</sub> = 0 the driver is off, so no current flows; zero load current needs V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>tn</sub>, giving V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>. Body effect raises that threshold, so V<sub>OH</sub> drops further. With V<sub>in</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> the load is saturated and the driver linear; equating the currents gives V<sub>OL</sub>, a few tenths of a volt.

Depletion load. An nMOS with a negative threshold (an extra channel implant) has drain at VDD, source at the output and gate at the source. Then VGS = 0 always and the device is on. While saturated it is a constant current source of value IDSS.

blocks.where: k<sub>nL</sub> is the load gain in A/V², V<sub>td</sub> the magnitude of the depletion threshold in volts (the threshold is −V<sub>td</sub>), k<sub>n</sub> and V<sub>tn</sub> belong to the driver, V<sub>OL</sub> is the output low voltage.

blocks.text: Now V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>. At V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> the load has V<sub>DS</sub> = 0 and carries no current, and the driver is off, so zero current satisfies both devices. As the output falls the load becomes a constant-current pull-up, so a modest driver already gives V<sub>OL</sub> below 0.1 V. The price is a process step and a load that is on whenever the output is low.
Pseudo-nMOS. A pMOS load: source at VDD, drain at the output, gate at ground. Then VGS = −VDD at all times, so it is a permanent current source and VOH = VDD. While the pMOS is saturated:

blocks.where: k<sub>p</sub> is the pMOS gain in A/V², V<sub>tp</sub> its threshold (negative, so |V<sub>tp</sub>| is its magnitude in volts), and the right side is the driver in the linear region.

blocks.text: VOL depends on the ratio kp/kn, not on absolute widths, so this is ratioed logic (3.7). A pMOS several times weaker than the driver keeps VOL a few tenths of a volt. Static current flows whenever the driver is on.

All four loads conduct while the output is low, which is exactly what the CMOS inverter avoids (3.1). They survive where one load is shared by a large pull-down network, as in wide NOR planes and PLAs, or as a weak keeper. Speed is discussed in 3.3.

figure.caption: The four ways to pull an NMOS inverter output up to V<sub>DD</sub>. All pass current while the output is low; they differ in output swing and load current.

spec.aria: A tree grouping the four NMOS inverter loads under one root: resistive, enhancement, depletion and pseudo-nMOS.

examples.question: A resistive-load NMOS inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, R<sub>L</sub> = 100 kΩ, driver k<sub>n</sub> = 20 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.8 V. The input is at 5 V. Find V<sub>OL</sub> and the static supply current.
steps: Input high: V<sub>GS</sub> = 5 V > 0.8 V, so the driver is on.
Try saturation: I<sub>D</sub> = 10 µA/V² × (4.2 V)² = 176.4 µA, which would drop 17.64 V across R<sub>L</sub>, more than V<sub>DD</sub>. So the driver is linear.
Driver: I<sub>D</sub> = 20 µA/V² × [4.2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2]. Resistor: I<sub>D</sub> = (5 − V<sub>OL</sub>)/100 kΩ.
Equate and multiply by 100 kΩ: 5 − V<sub>OL</sub> = 8.4V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>², so V<sub>OL</sub>² − 9.4V<sub>OL</sub> + 5 = 0.
Solve: V<sub>OL</sub> = (9.4 − √(88.36 − 20))/2 = (9.4 − 8.268)/2 = 0.566 V. The root 8.83 V lies above V<sub>DD</sub> and is rejected.
Check: 0.566 V < 4.2 V, so the linear assumption holds.
Static current: I = (5 − 0.566)/100 kΩ = 44.3 µA, so static power = 5 V × 44.3 µA = 0.22 mW.
examples.answer: V<sub>OL</sub> ≈ 0.57 V and the inverter draws 44.3 µA (0.22 mW) from the 5 V supply.
examples.check:
import math
VDD = 5.0
RL = 100e3
kn = 20e-6
Vtn = 0.8
A = kn * RL
a = A / 2
b = -(A * (VDD - Vtn) + 1)
c = VDD
V = (-b - math.sqrt(b * b - 4 * a * c)) / (2 * a)
print(round(V, 3))
print(round(V, 2))
I = (VDD - V) / RL
print(round(I * 1e6, 1))

traps: Using the saturation equation for the driver at the output low point. There V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>OL</sub> is much smaller than V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, so the driver is linear.
Forgetting the enhancement load loses a threshold: V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>, and body effect lowers it further.
Thinking a depletion load is off because V<sub>GS</sub> = 0. It carries I<sub>DSS</sub> and only stops at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0, when the output is at V<sub>DD</sub>.
Swapping source and drain of the load. In enhancement and depletion loads the source is the output node, so the load's V<sub>GS</sub> and V<sub>SB</sub> follow the output.

quiz.q: Name the four loads used with an NMOS inverter and one drawback shared by all four.
quiz.a: Resistive, enhancement nMOS, depletion nMOS and pseudo-nMOS. All draw static current while the output is low.

quiz.q: Why is the output high of an enhancement-load inverter V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub> rather than V<sub>DD</sub>?
quiz.a: The load gate is at V<sub>DD</sub> and its source is the output, so V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>out</sub>. With the driver off the load current must be zero, which needs V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>tn</sub>. Hence V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>tn</sub>; body effect raises V<sub>tn</sub>, so the high level falls further.

quiz.q: A depletion load has V<sub>GS</sub> = 0, yet the output high reaches the full V<sub>DD</sub>. Explain.
quiz.a: At V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> the load has V<sub>DS</sub> = 0, so it carries no current even with V<sub>GS</sub> = 0. The driver is off too, so zero current satisfies both devices. Below that point the load is a constant current source of I<sub>DSS</sub>.

quiz.q: In the worked example the supply current is 44.3 µA at V<sub>OL</sub> = 0.57 V and V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V. Find the static power of one gate and of 20,000 such gates.
quiz.a: P = V<sub>DD</sub> × I = 5 V × 44.3 µA = 0.22 mW per gate. For 20,000 gates, 0.22 mW × 20,000 = 4.4 W.

quiz.q: A depletion-load inverter has V<sub>DD</sub> = 5 V, I<sub>DSS</sub> = 20 µA, driver k<sub>n</sub> = 100 µA/V² and V<sub>tn</sub> = 0.8 V. Find V<sub>OL</sub>.
quiz.a: Equate: 20 µA = 100 µA/V² × [4.2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2], so 0.2 = 4.2V<sub>OL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub>²/2, giving V<sub>OL</sub>² − 8.4V<sub>OL</sub> + 0.4 = 0. Then V<sub>OL</sub> = (8.4 − √(70.56 − 1.6))/2 ≈ 0.048 V. This is below 4.2 V, so the linear assumption holds.

quiz.q: Why is pseudo-nMOS called ratioed logic, and what happens to V<sub>OL</sub> if the pMOS is made twice as strong?
quiz.a: V<sub>OL</sub> comes from balancing load current against driver current, so it depends on k<sub>p</sub>/k<sub>n</sub>, not on absolute sizes; scaling both widths changes nothing. Doubling k<sub>p</sub> doubles the pull-up current, so the driver must sink more and the output settles at a higher V<sub>OL</sub>, with double the static current.

quiz.q: How does the voltage transfer curve of a pseudo-nMOS inverter differ from that of a CMOS inverter, and what does that do to the two noise margins?
quiz.a: The weak pull-up makes the curve asymmetric, with the switching threshold well below V<sub>DD</sub>/2, and both V<sub>IL</sub> and V<sub>IH</sub> move to low input values. With V<sub>OH</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> the high noise margin V<sub>OH</sub> − V<sub>IH</sub> is large, but the low noise margin V<sub>IL</sub> − V<sub>OL</sub> is small.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pseudo-nMOS survives as the weak keeper that holds a dynamic node high, and as the single load shared by a large NOR plane in PLAs and memory arrays, where saving transistors matters more than static current. Depletion-mode devices appear in compound-semiconductor logic such as GaAs DCFL and in analog bias circuits.
